column1: The Inflation Attention Threshold and Inflation Surges

The thesis titled The Inflation Attention Threshold and Inflation Surges by Oliver Pfäuti  dated August 2024  explores the dynamics of public attention to inflation and its macroeconomic implications. At the onset of the recent inflation surge  public attention was initially low but increased rapidly as inflation rose. Pfäuti quantifies the changes in public attention to inflation  identifying an attention threshold at an inflation rate of approximately 4%. When inflation surpasses this threshold  public attention doubles. This heightened attention makes adverse supply shocks more inflationary  and the increased attention in 2021 is responsible for half of the subsequent supply-driven inflation. Pfäuti develops a model incorporating the attention threshold  demonstrating that typically short-lived shocks can lead to persistent inflation surges if they increase public attention. The attention threshold also prolongs the disinflation process after an inflation surge and introduces asymmetry in inflation dynamics.

The paper uses survey data from the University of Michigan’s Survey of Consumers (1978-2024) to estimate the attention threshold and levels in different regimes. It finds that attention is about 0.18 when inflation is below the threshold and nearly doubles to 0.35 when above it. A Markov-switching model confirms these findings  and similar results are obtained using regional data and the Survey of Consumer Expectations from the New York Fed. The study shows that there is only one attention threshold  and once controlled for  attention does not increase with inflation within a regime.

The attention regimes significantly impact inflation and inflation expectations dynamics. Using oil supply news shocks as a proxy for supply shocks  Pfäuti finds that inflation increases more than twice as much in response to these shocks in the high-attention regime compared to the low-attention regime. These effects are persistent  lasting one to two years. The attention threshold suggests that the U.S. economy entered the high-attention regime in early 2021. The increased attention accounts for about 55% of the inflation surge from early 2021 to mid-2022. Without the attention increase  the inflation surge would have been significantly smaller.

The paper concludes that understanding and accounting for changes in public attention to inflation is crucial for explaining recent inflation dynamics and the interplay between inflation and inflation expectations. The findings have important implications for monetary policy  suggesting that managing public attention could be as crucial as managing inflation expectations themselves.
